ABSTRACT

Medical imaging plays an important role in the early detection and treatment of brain tumours. However due to reduced availability of neurosurgeons in Nigeria , manually segmenting tumour regions and classifying tumour types can be time consuming and prone to inconsistencies. This project addresses these challenges by developing a multi-task learning model that performs both tumour segmentation and classification using Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) data. The multi-task model uses an adaptive loss balancing algorithm to optimize both tasks simultaneously without compromising accuracy. EfficientNet-B0 is employed for tumour classification, while a U-Net architecture is used for segmentation. The BraTS MRI 2020 dataset and the Figshare Brain MRI Dataset are used for training and evaluation. This project followed a comprehensive approach including data extraction, pre- processing, model design, training and evaluation. Results show that the adaptive loss mechanism improves task coordination, with the model achieving strong performance in both segmentation (based on Dice scores) and classification (based on accuracy and F1-score), validating the effectiveness of the multi-task setup.
Keywords: Medical Imaging, Multi-task Learning, Segmentation, Classification, Loss Balancing,   MRI Image
CHAPTER ONE
INTRODUCTION
1.1 	 Background Information

With the rise of machine learning, various methods have emerged for training neural networks such as transfer learning, supervised learning, reinforcement learning and multi-task learning (Ryu et al., 2023). While multi-task learning has unique advantages it is not as popular as other training methods and is much less frequently utilized, as many practitioners prefer to train separate neural networks for distinct task (Ryu et al., 2023). Multi-task learning focuses on training a single neural network to perform multiple, related tasks simultaneously, which offers significant benefits in terms of computational power and resource efficiency (Lee & Son, 2022). By sharing representations between tasks, multi-task learning can lead to better generalization and improved performance with lower computational costs (Li et al., 2023).

Even though multi-task learning (MTL) offers several advantages like reduced training time and better data efficiency, it also presents several challenges that can hinder its effectiveness. One challenge highlighted is the varying learning rates required by different tasks (Standley et al., 2019). Another important problem is the balancing of loss functions from individual tasks during training (Du et al., 2024). If these issues are not properly managed, one task may dominate the others during the training process and lead to a sub-par performance across all tasks (Standley et al., 2019). Providing proper attention to every task is the key to reach the best performance, and attempting to reconcile these tasks is still a major issue in the multi-task learning settings.

The tumour segmentation and classification multi-task model integrated an adaptive loss balancing algorithm to deal with the mentioned issues. This algorithm was able to dynamically balance the losses associated with each task. The algorithm did this by assigning weights to the two tasks based on the perceived degree of difficulty and dynamically adjusting the weights during the training process. This approach builds on promising results from related domains, where dynamic adjustments have shown potential to improve training efficiency and task performance (Song et al., 2022).

Existing literature shows that the conventional loss balancing approaches have been static in many cases and they do not respond to the dynamism of multi-task training (Lin et al., 2023). The conventional approaches have concentrated on the manipulation of forward pass of the network or optimization of the architecture without targeting the ultimate problem of gradient imbalances throughout the backpropagation (Chen et al., 2017). Such imbalances may adversely affect training by causing training tasks to cause gradients with large, unbalanced magnitudes. The adaptive loss balancing algorithm used in this project bridges this gap by adapting the weights on tasks to ensure that the learning is balanced to offer a more comprehensive solution to the problem specific to multi-task learning.

The adaptive loss balancing strategy guaranteed a more balanced learning between the two tasks, and this strategy resulted in a better accuracy in the two tasks. The significance of this research lies not only in its potential to advance the field of multi-task learning but also in its applicability to various domains where similar challenges exist, thereby contributing to more effective machine learning solutions in healthcare and other fields .
1.2  	Statement of the Problem

The multi-task learning approach offers high potential for resource-efficient neural networks by enabling them to perform multiple related tasks within a single model (Zhai et al., 2024). This efficiency is especially critical in resource-constrained sectors like neurosurgery, where there is often a shortage of skilled professionals and tools to analyse large volumes of complex medical data (Morgan & Nwatuzor, 2020). However, this method faces a critical challenge which is balancing task performance effectively during training.

Previously, conventional multi-task models often relied on fixed-weight loss functions, assigning equal weights to all tasks or relying on static assumptions about their relative importance (Chen et al., 2017). Although this static approach is simple, it did not suffice when it comes to dealing with the relative complexities and changing needs of tasks in training. Consequently, some of the work would tend to finish quicker than others, resulting in poor overall performance and an unbalanced model (Liu et al., 2022).

In recent years, however, dynamic loss-balancing algorithms have emerged as a solution to this problem. To overcome the shortcomings of the static methods, dynamic methods like dynamic weight adjustments, uncertainty weighting, and gradient-based methods like gradient normalization have been designed (Gong et al., 2019). These algorithms adaptively adjust loss weights during training, ensuring that each task receives the attention it requires based on real-time conditions. Dynamic balancing approaches offer great improvement in performance and stability of multi-task learning systems by considering the factors such as task difficulty, training dynamics, and conflicting gradients.

This study built an enhanced multi-task model specifically designed for MRI brain tumour segmentation and classification. The nature of tasks being trained in a multi-task environment is crucial in determining the most appropriate loss-balancing strategy (Standley et al., 2019). For instance, tasks with conflicting gradients may benefit from gradient-based methods like GradNorm, which normalize gradients across tasks to ensure consistent optimization (Chen et al., 2017). Meanwhile, tasks with uncertain difficulty are better suited to uncertainty weighting, which adjusts loss weights based on task confidence (Liu et al., 2022). Additionally, tasks that evolve dynamically during training, as is common with medical imaging data, may require strategies like dynamic weighting to adapt to these shifts (Li et al., 2023). By tailoring the algorithm to the specific characteristics of the segmentation and classification tasks, this study optimizes multi-task performance and provide insights for broader applications in medical and other domains.

1.6 	Scope of the Study

This study focused on building a multi-task deep learning model for brain tumour segmentation and classification, with an emphasis on designing an adaptive loss balancing algorithm to optimize the model's performance. The primary goal was to construct a shared encoder-decoder architecture, where a shared encoder extracts features from MRI scans, followed by two task-specific heads: one for segmentation using a SwinUNet based architecture and another for classification using EfficientNet. The adaptive loss balancing algorithm was integrated into the multi-task learning process to dynamically adjust task specific weights based on performance metrics, such as loss magnitudes, uncertainty scores, and convergence rates. This ensured that both the segmentation and classification task received optimal contributions during training, preventing one from dominating the other and this lead to an overall improved model performance.

This study evaluated the multi-task model by benchmarking it against existing multi-task models that perform both brain tumour segmentation and classification using the standard datasets. Standard performance metrics such as accuracy and IoU for segmentation, and accuracy and F1-score for classification were used for comparison.

Furthermore, the multi-task model was integrated into a web application, which allowed for real-time analysis of MRI scans for both segmentation and classification tasks. The web application was developed using a Flask backend and React for the frontend interface, facilitating an interactive and user-friendly platform for medical professionals. Usability testing was conducted in a clinical setting to assess the system's usefulness and interface quality, ensuring that the web application provides a practical tool for real-world medical imaging and diagnosis.

CHAPTER TWO 
LITERATURE REVIEW
2.1 	 Preamble

This chapter provides a literature review of the core concepts, the general problem space, and the specific domain under review. It proceeds to explore key concepts that are important in the development of a multi-task model using adaptive loss balancing as well as the relevant architectures for implementing segmentation and classification of MRI brain scans. The review also explores a list of existing solutions and systems that have been used to solve similar problems in the problem space, establishing a platform for the project's approach.
2.2   	Review of Multi-task Learning

Multi-task learning (MTL) is a machine learning sub-field that improves learning efficiency and prediction accuracy by training models on multiple related tasks simultaneously using a shared representation (Lee & Son, 2022). Inspired by human learning, where skills from one task can aid another. MTL seeks to leverage the knowledge gained in one task to enhance the generalization performance of others (Li et al., 2023). By enabling tasks to share domain-specific insights, MTL reduces the need for large, task-specific datasets while enhancing overall model performance.

According to Richard Caruana, multi-task learning was introduced long before the introduction of deep learning , but the strong learned features within deep networks and their excellent single-task performance have kindled renewed interest (Chen et al., 2017). Although the primary focus of this study is medical imaging, multi-task learning has applications in many other fields, from natural language processing and speech synthesis, to very domain-specific applications such as traffic prediction (Lin et al., 2023).

MTL is often compared to related paradigms such as transfer learning, multi-label learning, and multi-output regression. While transfer learning focuses on improving a specific target task using knowledge from source tasks, MTL treats all tasks equally, aiming to optimize performance for all simultaneously (Standley et al., 2019). In contrast to transfer learning’s task prioritization, MTL’s uniform focus ensures that knowledge is bidirectional and not confined to a single target task (Obonyo & Ruiru, 2019).

MTL's power lies in its use of inductive transfer learning, where representations are shared across tasks to improve performance, particularly in data-scarce or goal-correlated settings (Nisar et al., 2023). In medical imaging, for example, MTL models can be used to classify MRI scans for the presence of tumours and simultaneously segment tumour regions, transferring knowledge between tasks to improve overall accuracy (Rabby et al., 2024). Such multi-tasking not only reduces computational overhead but also makes applications with limited data and resources simpler.

However, practitioners must carefully consider two things prior to the use of MTL: what to share and how to share (Standley et al., 2019). It is important to determine which tasks can be trained together, since tasks must be complementary and not opposing in order to benefit from shared learning (Nisar et al., 2023). In addition, it is essential to decide what knowledge to transfer during training, i.e., features, parameters, or representations, to enable efficient transfer and minimize interference between tasks (Gong et al., 2019).

Despite its advantages, MTL is faced with challenges like overfitting and task balancing (Hervella et al., 2024). In some cases, a task can dominate the learning process, resulting in poorer performance for the remaining tasks (Standley et al., 2019). This is especially difficult in scenarios with opposing gradients, where the optimization of one task has a detrimental effect on another (Nisar et al., 2023). MTL models also usually require complex architectures and hyperparameter searching, making them computationally expensive and harder to use for real-world applications (Zhang & Yang, 2017).

Recent advances, such as adaptive loss balancing algorithms, address these limitations by updating task weights iteratively to encourage balanced learning (Song et al., 2022). These improvements ensure that all tasks benefit equally from the learning process, enhancing the use of MTL across applications (Hervella et al., 2024). As research continues, the potential of MTL only increases, and it is now a cornerstone of modern machine learning methodologies.
2.3	Review of Loss Balancing

Loss balancing, in the context of multi-task learning (MTL), refers to the process of managing the relative importance of tasks by adjusting each task's loss function (Zhang & Yang, 2017). The primary goal is to prevent some tasks from dominating the learning process at the expense of the performance of other tasks. This is particularly important when the tasks differ in their levels of difficulty or when the data distributions between tasks are not balanced (Nisar et al., 2023). Balancing the losses ensures that each task has its own equitable contribution to the overall learning, which leads to generalization and task performance improvement.

The requirement for loss balancing in MTL is because the range of loss can be different for different tasks, and hence some tasks can overwhelm the others while training. For instance, in an MTL model where both tasks are to classify MRI images and also segment the same images, the segmentation task will naturally have a higher loss due to its finer granularity. When both tasks are being trained using a fixed, imbalanced loss function, the model may end up paying more attention to the task with the higher loss at the expense of the other task. Therefore, dynamic loss balancing is required to ensure that all tasks are optimally trained and not one of them dominates the others (Nisar et al., 2023).

Historically, loss balancing in MTL originated with the discovery of MTL itself (Jaradat et al., 2024). Static methods of loss balancing depended on pre-defined weights for each task according to domain knowledge or empirical study (Gong et al., 2019). Nevertheless, this method was not optimal because it was not flexible in changing the loss balance during training. One of the very first loss balancing efforts was done through the early work of Rich Caruana in the 1990s, when he introduced the idea of multi-task learning (Chen et al., 2017). Although early methods simply utilized uniform weights to ensemble the losses from multiple tasks, as research evolved, scientists sensed the need for more sophisticated, adaptive strategies (Gong et al., 2019).

The evolution from static to dynamic loss balancing began in earnest with the introduction of uncertainty weighting (UW) by Gong et al. (2019). Uncertainty weighting was one of the first methods to adaptively adjust the importance of each task during training based on the uncertainty of the task. The idea behind uncertainty weighting is that tasks with higher uncertainty should be given more weight as they require more attention during training (Song et al., 2022). This approach was a step in the direction of more adaptive, data-dependent methods for loss balancing, where the task weights could be changed in real time based on the learning process.

A paper by Gong et al. (2019) categorizes loss functions into two broad categories: Pure loss functions and gradient based functions. Pure loss techniques include Uncertainty weighting (Cipolla et al., 2018) and Dynamic weighting average (DWA) while gradient-based loss includes Gradient Normalisation (Chen et al., 2017), Multiple gradient descent algorithm (McCaughan et al., 2023), Projecting Conflicting Gradient, Gradient Sign Dropout, Impartial Multi task learning (Yuan & Zhang, 2023) and Gradient Vaccine. This research intends to focus on pure loss functions since the two tasks being trained together, segmentation and classification, are related and do not have very opposing gradients. Also, the pure loss methods discussed above are simpler to apply and enjoy common usage and acceptance (Song et al., 2022).As the research area advances, more sophistication in balancing losses is anticipated, enabling MTL models to attain even better performance on varied tasks.
2.4   	Review of Relevant Concepts
This section details the various concepts that are relevant to this project. They include:
2.4.1      Artificial Intelligence

Artificial intelligence (AI) applies computational algorithms to analyse and comprehend complex datasets. AI is transforming medical diagnostics in imaging operations (for segmentation: specifying constituents, whole or partial, and diagnosing, and classification: identifying similarity, similarity, and potential for disaster), though its primary objective is to mimic cognitive operations like learning, reasoning, and self-refreshing (Tian et al., 2023). AI uses patterns from enormous databases of tagged images beyond medicine, and its phenomenal speed, efficiency, and accuracy in generating probability predictions over a wide spectrum (any prediction model will have variables) has profound implications for future diagnostic accuracy and treatment.

In the specific field of MRI brain scan diagnostic image analysis, AI algorithms can classify brain tumours, identify brain injury, and predict possible future status for certain neurological diseases (Kaur et al., 2020). For example, they can tell whether a tumour is benign or malignant by noticing subtle differences in an MRI image. Segmentation of various brain structures can be done using AI on the brain as a whole, and in segments, which may be beneficial for everyone for the measurement of total brain volume, abnormalities, and then preparation for a surgical procedure (Kaur et al., 2020). If AI can perform these steps for the radiologist, it can save the radiologist a lot of time and let them focus on harder cases.

The use of AI in MRI brain scan analysis offers several benefits. Firstly, it can improve the accuracy and speed of diagnosis, leading to earlier interventions and better patient outcomes (Kaur et al., 2020).  Secondly, AI can help to standardize diagnostic criteria, reducing inter-observer variability and ensuring more consistent results across different healthcare settings. Thirdly, AI can uncover hidden patterns in MRI data that may not be readily apparent to human observers, potentially leading to new insights into the diagnosis and treatment of neurological disorders.

While AI has great potential in medical imaging, it comes with several challenges. One of them is the transparency of how some AI algorithms arrive at their conclusions, which is sometimes called the "black box" problem. This openness can deter clinicians to have faith and utilize these systems. The second issue is making sure that AI models are trained on a wide range of datasets so that they are unbiased and provide the same results to patients from various groups. Legal and ethical considerations, including patient privacy and confidentiality, as well as liability for incorrect diagnoses, also must be met with serious deliberation (Kaur et al., 2020).
2.4.2     Machine Learning

Machine learning (ML) is a branch of artificial intelligence (AI) that centres on creating algorithms and statistical models that enable computers to learn and improve from data without explicit programming. These systems analyse input data to make predictions or decisions, with their accuracy improving as they are exposed to more information. The learning process involves training algorithms on extensive datasets, fine-tuning their parameters to enhance performance in specific tasks. ML tasks are categorized as supervised (using labelled datasets), unsupervised (identifying patterns in unlabelled data), or semi-supervised (a mix of labelled and unlabelled data) (Zhai et al., 2024).

Machine learning (ML) is crucial in medical imaging, leveraging technologies such as Xrays, MRI, cardiac MRI , Computed Topography (CT) scans, mammograms, and histopathological images  to aid in diagnosing and treating diseases. In the context of MRI brain scans, ML algorithms excel at tasks like classification and segmentation, enabling the identification of brain tumours, damaged regions, and disease progression. Supervised learning methods, such as Support Vector Machines (SVMs) and Neural Networks, are particularly effective when trained on labelled datasets to handle classification and regression tasks (Yang et al., 2024). For instance, SVMs classify tumours and differentiate between healthy and diseased brain tissues by determining the optimal hyperplane in the feature space. Neural Networks, modelled after the human brain, comprise interconnected neurons that can identify intricate patterns in imaging data. These networks are widely used for image classification and segmentation, making them indispensable tools in radiology (Zhai et al., 2024).

Unsupervised learning, unlike supervised learning, deals with unlabelled data to discover patterns and groupings. Techniques such as K-means clustering are used to group data points based on similarity, which is particularly useful in medical imaging for segmenting MRI scans, such as isolating tumours from healthy brain tissue (Yang et al., 2024). Dimensionality reduction methods, like Principal Component Analysis (PCA), streamline the analysis by reducing the number of features while retaining critical information, which enhances the efficiency of MRI scan processing by minimizing noise (Zhai et al., 2024).

Deep learning, a specialized subset of ML, utilizes deep neural networks to process complex datasets such as medical images. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are tailored for grid-structured data like images and are effective in tasks such as image classification, segmentation, and object detection. Transfer learning, which involves fine-tuning pre-trained models on specific tasks, is particularly valuable in medical imaging where labelled datasets are limited. This method enables models to transfer knowledge from general domains to specific applications, like MRI brain scan analysis (Yang et al., 2024). Additionally, Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), which are designed for sequential data, can be applied to longitudinal MRI studies for tracking disease progression over time.

However, challenges remain in integrating ML into medical imaging. The opaque black box nature of some ML models can hinder trust among clinicians and patients, emphasizing the need for Explainable AI to clarify how predictions are made (Yang et al., 2024). Ethical considerations include ensuring algorithms are unbiased, safeguarding patient privacy, and integrating solutions seamlessly into clinical workflows. Practical challenges, such as training healthcare providers, meeting regulatory standards, and addressing the high computational demands of ML models, also require attention. Successfully overcoming these hurdles can significantly enhance diagnostic precision, foster personalized treatment, and improve overall patient care.
2.4.3     Deep Learning

Deep learning (DL) is a niche field within machine learning that leverages artificial neural networks with several layers to detect intricate patterns and features from data (Zakaria et al., 2022). The networks possess the hierarchical composition of the human brain, capturing progressively abstract representations as data moves through each layer. DL algorithms achieve state-of-the-art performance in tasks like image classification, natural language processing, and medical image analysis.

In medical imaging, DL has been particularly useful in interpreting complicated images such as MRI brain scans. The models are capable of classification and segmentation, which are crucial steps in diagnosing and monitoring neurological conditions. For example, they can classify brain tumours, segment structures for volumetric analysis or anomaly detection, and predict disease progression for conditions such as Alzheimer's (Zakaria et al., 2022). By accelerating and enhancing diagnosis, DL plays a vital role in more accurate treatment planning and better patient outcomes.

Model selection is both dataset and task-specific. For example, given the temporal characteristics of functional MRI data, RNNs are most appropriate for functional MRI data analysis, whereas CNNs are most appropriate for applications such as tumour classification and structural segmentation. Transfer learning, i.e., fine-tuning pre-trained networks to small datasets, is especially useful where medical imaging data is available in small quantities (Obonyo & Ruiru, 2019).

However, DL in medical imaging is confronted with challenges in interpretability, need for large and varied datasets, and ethical concerns in patient confidentiality and data utilization. Regardless of such challenges, DL development continues to make an impact in personalised medicine and diagnostics accuracy. To surmount such challenges and realize the complete transformational promise of DL, more research has to be done in medical imaging (Zakaria et al., 2022).
2.4.4       Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN’s)

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are specialized deep learning models that automatically learn and extract task-relevant features from visual data, including images (Khozeimeh et al., 2021). Their layered structure consists of activation functions like ReLU to introduce non-linearity for improved pattern learning, pooling layers to reduce data dimensions while maintaining important information, and convolutional layers that use filters to identify patterns in input images. Batch normalisation guarantees stable learning by normalising data within batches, while dropout regularisation avoids overfitting by deactivating random neurones during training.

CNNs are excellent at classification and segmentation in medical imaging, especially for MRI brain scans. By identifying unique features in images, they are able to classify conditions such as Alzheimer's or brain tumours. They help with tasks like measuring tumour volume or planning surgeries by accurately defining regions of interest, such as tumours or particular brain tissues (Khozeimeh et al., 2021). LeNet, AlexNet, GoogLeNet, and ResNet are well-known CNN architectures that have shown remarkable success in medical image analysis because of their distinctive design optimisations.

While CNNs hold great promise in medical imaging, challenges like limited data availability, model interpretability, and generalization persist. Researchers are addressing these issues by integrating multi-tasking approaches, embedding clinical expertise, and developing explainable AI solutions to enhance the adoption of CNNs in clinical settings and revolutionize brain disorder diagnosis and treatment (Khozeimeh et al., 2021).
2.4.5     Semantic Segmentation with SwinUnet

Semantic segmentation is a valuable medical image analysis application in which each pixel is given a meaningful label, which is critical for identifying key areas such as tumours, organs, and lesions. SwinUNet, a U-shaped Transformer-type model, has great promise for this, using the Swin Transformer block for semantic information long-range interaction (Cao et al., 2021). SwinUNet's architecture consists of an encoder, bottleneck, decoder, and skip connections, which are all constructed based on the Swin Transformer block, characterized by the presence of shifted windows. This enables the efficient computation of self-attention  via cyclic shifting, consequently facilitating the encoding of local and global information that is required for precise segmentation (Cao et al., 2021).

In SwinUNet, the encoder processes the medical images by dividing them into non-overlapping patches, which are treated as tokens. These patches are then fed into the Swin Transformer blocks to produce hierarchical feature representations. The decoder is symmetric to this, using Swin Transformer blocks and patch expanding layers for up sampling. Skip connections, like in the initial U-Net, help connect multi-scale features from encoder to decoder, which makes the segmentation predictions finer and prevents information loss due to down sampling (Cao et al., 2021). The ability of skip connections to connect different levels of feature representations enhances the model's performance regarding the removal of fine-grained details and the improvement of segmentation accuracy (Cao et al., 2021).

SwinUNet has achieved the state of the art performance on several medical image segmentation tasks, such as multi-organ and cardiac segmentation. It surpasses conventional CNN-based methods in its potential to learn fine features and predict edges better. It also exhibits outstanding generalization, with superior performance on a range of imaging modalities including CT and MRI, and thus is a very useful tool for medical image analysis (Cao et al., 2021).
2.4.6      Classification with EfficientNet

EfficientNet is a family of CNNs that are designed to achieve the best possible performance for image classification for a fixed amount of computation. The model achieves state of the art performance by a novel scaling method whereby the depth, width, and resolution of the network are all scaled in a consistent manner to balance between resources (Mutreja & Bittner, 2025). Its secret to success lies in its compound scaling method, under the supervision of Neural Architecture Search, which adjusts each dimension's scaling coefficients to reach a balance between accuracy and computational efficiency (Mutreja & Bittner, 2025).

EfficientNet architecture includes Mobile Inverted Bottleneck Convolution modules that are responsible for its efficiency. These modules apply depthwise separable convolutions, inverted residual blocks, and Squeeze-and-Excitation attention to achieve the highest feature extraction while minimizing computation cost (Tan & Le, 2019). This allows the network to achieve good performance with fewer parameters and computations, which is particularly convenient in medical imaging tasks, where the complexity of data might be high.

When using EfficientNet for such tasks as MRI brain scan classification, the architecture can be modified to suit the particular nature of medical imaging data. Pre-training the network on large datasets like ImageNet can enable the network to learn good features prior to fine-tuning it on small annotated MRI image datasets (Trinh et al., 2022). This transfer learning has been capable of improving accuracy, particularly while dealing with small training data, as in the case of medical imaging.

For classifying brain tumours, we would need a pre-labelled dataset with ground truth labels, which include No Tumour, Glioma, Meningioma, and Pituitary tumours. These labelled classes act as the reference for the network to learn from so that the model learns to classify MRI scans correctly. By reducing prediction errors by supervised learning, EfficientNet is able to generalize to novel, unseen medical images and thus represents a useful tool for automated tumour classification in clinical environments (Tan & Le, 2019).
2.5	Review of Related Works
This section details the  previous studies and works that are related to this project. They include:
2.5.1	Dynamic Restrained Uncertainty Weighting Loss for Multi-task Learning of
Vocal Expression

Song et al. (2022) presents a new approach that benefits from Uncertainty Weighting and Dynamic Weight Average. The authors also propose a conservative weighting strategy to improve the explainability of learning, which is based on a lean multi-exit CNN model (Song et al., 2022). The main advantage of this approach is that it introduces uncertainty estimation to focus the learning process on more relevant tasks without incurring interference from less important ones. This dynamic weighting brings about increased adaptability and efficiency of the model in multi-task environments.

A weakness that might then exist is the dependence on the accurate estimation of uncertainty for each of the tasks. This is computationally expensive at times and not very reliable when data quality is low or tasks within the model are very heterogeneous. All these weaknesses can potentially compromise the model's efficiency and robustness in particular environments.
2.5.2	AHU-MultiNet: Adaptive Loss balancing Based on Homoscedastic Uncertainty in Multi-task Medical Image Segmentation Networks

Liu et al. (2022) introduces an inter-task consistency mechanism to explore the intrinsic information of images and regularize predictions in the correct direction. The study suggested a multi-task network with three tasks, including predicting probabilistic segmentation maps, signed distance maps (SDMs), and binary edge maps during training (Liu et al., 2022). It applies an adaptive loss balancing method that leverages the homoscedastic uncertainties of different tasks as a confidence measure to decide on the loss weight of each task (Shan et al., 2022). Homoscedastic uncertainty of every task, taken as a noise parameter, is updated using backpropagation during training. Here, surprisingly, the homoscedastic uncertainty reduces with the weight of its corresponding task increasing, i.e., harder tasks (with higher noise or uncertainty) have smaller weights and easier or more certain tasks have larger weights. It is an automatic process in which the three tasks are ideally balanced by the network, reaching the optimal training state faster and performing better than uniform weighting. While this approach stabilizes training and prevents noisy tasks from dominating the process, it also can lead to suboptimal learning for these harder tasks, as they receive less attention in training.
2.5.3	GradNorm: Gradient Normlaization for Adaptive Loss Balancing in
Deep Multi-task Networks

Chen et al. (2017) presents a gradient normalization method which  balances training in deep multi-task models by dynamically scaling gradient magnitudes. GradNorm is more precise and less overfitting than singletask networks, static baselines, and adaptive multi-task loss balancing algorithms (Chen et al., 2017). GradNorm establishes a common scale for gradient magnitudes and also adapts training rates for different tasks in a manner that a task is not converged before the other, which could lead to overfitting. However, one of the downsides of this approach is that in multi-task learning, there are sometimes conflicting gradients from the different tasks, especially when the tasks have opposing goals or values. This may result in training instability or degrade model performance because the model will not be able to balance the conflicting gradients. Thus, while GradNorm attempts to normalize gradients for balanced learning, the potential for conflict between gradients remains an issue, and therefore the method is more complex and potentially unstable than methods based solely on loss.
2.5.4	BT-Net:An End-to-End Multi-task Architecture for Brain Tumour
Classification, Segmentation, and Localization from MRI Images.

Rabby et al. (2024) proposed a new multi-task network based on the default VGG16, and a U-Net variant concatenation that is capable of segmentation, classification, and localization simultaneously with the same architecture. The classification branch was trained using the Brain Tumour MRI Dataset, while the segmentation branch was trained using the Brain Tumour Segmentation dataset (Rabby et al., 2024). The research utilized the Adam optimizer for segmentation and the stochastic gradient descent optimization algorithm for classification. The research fails to mention, however, the utilization of any loss balancing methods to control and balance the tasks of segmentation, classification, and localization in its multi-task architecture, which may result in problems with the efficient training of the model.
2.5.5	Dual-Balancing for Multi-task Learning

Lin et al. (2023) proposes a double balancing method to solve the problem of task balancing on both loss and gradient sides to ensure that no single task dominates the process of learning (Lin et al., 2023). To simulate loss-scale balancing, the study applies a logarithm transformation to each task loss in an attempt to ensure that all task losses are of the same scale (Lin et al., 2023). This addresses the issue of tasks with opposing loss functions undergoing different scales, which can lead to imbalances during training. Similarly, Dual-Balancing for Multi-task Learning, employs gradient-magnitude balancing by normalizing all task gradients to possess an equal magnitude as the maximum gradient norm (Lin et al., 2023). This is to prevent the deep gradients of individual tasks from overwhelming the update direction of shared model parameters and thus facilitate more equitable contributions per task. While DB-MTL presents encouraging performance in addressing the task balancing problem, Further research might be needed to assess the efficiency of the approach in scenarios with a large number of tasks or considerably different tasks and also with regard to the sensitivity of the approach to hyperparameter tuning.
2.5.6	PS-MTL-LUCAS: A partially shared multi-task learning model for
simultaneously predicting multiple soil properties

Zhai et al. (2024) introduces a multi-task learning (MTL) model that is capable of predicting multiple soil properties simultaneously using Vis-NIR spectroscopy data. The key feature of PS-MTL-LUCAS is the adoption of partially shared layer architecture. As compared to hard parameter sharing and soft parameter sharing structures commonly applied in the MTL model, PS-MTL-LUCAS brings forth a unique shared layer learned regarding the general representations that unify all tasks without loss of task-specific layers for particular property prediction values (Zhai et al., 2024). This partially shared structure is targeted at enhancing performance by enabling information exchange between layers and minimizing costs of communication during training (Zhai et al., 2024). The authors really express the efficiency of PS-MTL-LUCAS as it proceeds to carry out intensive tests in the LUCAS topsoil dataset against competing state-of-the-art models for soil property prediction, which included pH, N, OC, and CaCO36. However, further research can be conducted to explore its potential limitations, such as difficulties in optimizing the interaction between shared and task-specific layers or difficulties in scaling the model to a larger number of soil properties.
2.5.7	Multi-Adaptive Optimization for multi-task learning with deep neural networks

Hervella et al. ​(2024) ​introduces ​a ​new ​method ​known ​as ​Multi-Adaptive Optimization(MAO) for multi-task deep neural network training optimization of task contributions. Instead of per-task weighting coefficients over losses or gradients, MAO dynamically adjusts the effective learning rate for each task per network parameter (Hervella et al., 2024). This attempts to provide parameter updates with a balanced characterization by normalizing the global learning rate with the strength of each task's supervisory signal, measured using the exponential moving average of squared gradients. This method is combined with the Adam optimization algorithm and tested on a number of computer vision tasks, showing better performance than alternative task-balancing techniques. The one drawback is the linear complexity with the number of tasks because of the independent calculation of updates and gradients for every task. This might be computationally demanding when training with many tasks. Future research could explore ways of enhancing the computational efficiency of MAO in such domains.

2.7	Gaps Identified in Literature

While the reviewed studies demonstrate various approaches to multi-task learning (MTL) and loss balancing in medical image processing, they reveal several gaps in the literature concerning loss balancing methods and architectures for multi-task learning (MTL). While MTL offers potential benefits over single-task learning by leveraging shared knowledge across tasks, effectively balancing task contributions and optimizing information sharing remain active areas of research (S. Zhai et al., 2024).

One gap lies in the limited exploration of static loss balancing methods in the context of MTL. Although the sources categorize traditional algorithms in cloud computing as static, this classification is not extended to loss balancing techniques for machine learning (Lin et al., 2023). Static loss balancing, involving fixed weights assigned to each task's loss throughout training, contrasts with adaptive methods that dynamically adjust weights based on factors or variables discovered during training, including:  task performance, uncertainty, or gradients. Even though static loss balancing methods are relatively simple, they have not received much attention in literature, leaving their effectiveness and potential benefits unexamined.

While the papers mention various approaches, including uncertainty weighting (UW) (Song et al., 2022), dynamic weight average, and impartial multi-task learning  (Lin et al., 2023), they acknowledge that these methods often fail to achieve satisfactory results. Many existing approaches struggle to prevent one task from dominating the learning process, leading to uneven performance across tasks. This limitation highlights the need for more robust and adaptive loss balancing techniques that can effectively handle the complexities of task relationships in MTL.

During the course of the literature review, various limitations in typical ML architectures were  pointed out especially, hard and soft parameter sharing (Zhai et al., 2024). Even though hard parameter sharing is simple and effective it can be less accurate when task relationships are conflicting. While soft parameter sharing, is prone to scalability issues as the number of tasks increases (Zhai et al., 2024). The paper exploring PS-MTL-LUCAS for soil property prediction proposes a partially shared architecture to address these limitations. However, finding the optimal balance between shared layers and task-specific layers remains an area for further exploration. This gap in the literature shows the need to develop innovative MTL architectures that can  take advantage of task relationships while ensuring scalability and good performance across different tasks.

Finally, the papers reviewed show the importance of integrating domain-specific knowledge and considerations into the design of MTL models. In the paper focusing on brain tumour classification and segmentation, the authors emphasize the need to evaluate MTL models with expert radiologists to measure their accuracy and real-world applicability (Rabby et al., 2024). Similarly, the discussion on soil property prediction acknowledges the importance of balancing model performance with the practicality of data acquisition, suggesting the need to consider the cost and dimensionality of Vis-NIR spectroscopy data (Rabby et al., 2024). These insights suggest a gap in the literature concerning the integration of domain-specific knowledge into MTL model development and evaluation. This includes understanding the unique challenges and limitations within specific application areas, such as healthcare in order to tailor MTL models for real-world deployment and ensure practical use.
2.8	Summary of Literature Review

The papers reviewed in this chapter exhaustively explore the domain of multi-task learning as well as the various loss-balancing techniques that can be applied to it. Multi-task learning is a very broad field; therefore it is impossible to exhaust all existing literature. The works reviewed in this chapter focus on the problem of balancing task-specific losses during the training of a multi-task model. These studies highlight many methods of solving this problem including dynamic weight adjustment, uncertainty weighting, gradient normalization, dual balancing and experimenting with different model architectures to achieve an optimal balance (Hervella et al., 2024).

The literature review also identifies some gaps in our current understanding of multi-task learning and loss balancing. Even with the many existing approaches to task balancing, achieving consistently accurate results across all tasks remains a problem. This emphasizes the need for a more adaptable and dynamic approach that can handle the complex relationships between tasks. Additionally, the review emphasizes the importance of real-world practical considerations. For example, in medical applications, multi-task learning models should be evaluated in collaboration with medical experts to ensure reliability and interpretability.

3.3	Model Development

The main aim of this project was to develop a multi-task deep learning architecture capable of learning to classify and segment brain tumours from MRI scans. The following sub headings in this section detail the step by step methodology taken to build the multi-task model and integrate it into a functional web application.
3.3.1	Data Collection and Pre-processing

This section details the data sources, pre-processing procedures, and dataset preparation methods used to ensure that the model could accurately perform both classification and segmentation tasks. To effectively train the multi-task model for both classification and segmentation of brain tumours, a Comma Separated Value (CSV) file comprising of brain MRI images, corresponding segmentation masks, and classification labels was prepared and used to train the model. The data collection process involved sourcing from two standard publicly available datasets, followed by a series of pre-processing steps to ensure consistency during model training.
3.3.2	Data Sources
To achieve the dual task of classification and segmentation, two standard datasets were used:

BraTS 2020 Dataset: The BraTS 2020 dataset is sourced from the Brain Tumour Segmentation Challenge (BraTS), this dataset consists of high-resolution 3D MRI volumes with expert annotated tumour segmentation masks. For this project, axial slices from the T1ce (contrast-enhanced) modality were extracted and converted into 2D images, which are suited for training a 2D U-Net for semantic segmentation. The segmentation masks are binary, marking tumour versus background at the pixel level.

Figshare Brain MRI Dataset: This dataset contains over 3,000 2D MRI images labelled into four categories: glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumour, and no tumour. Each image is already labelled at the image level, making it ideal for training the classification branch of the model. Although the images vary in size and appearance, they have been curated for clarity and balanced class distribution.
3.3.3	Metadata Compilation
To align both segmentation and classification information, a consolidated CSV file named updated_labelled_dataset.csv was created. Each row in the CSV includes:
image_path: the file path to the MRI slice.
mask_path: the file path to the corresponding segmentation mask (for BraTS dataset).
label: the label indicating the category type the tumour falls in (for classification).
3.3.4	Dataset Splitting
The dataset was divided into three parts:
Training Set (70%): Used to fit the model and update weights.
Validation Set (15%): Used during training to monitor model generalization and prevent overfitting.
Test Set (15%): Held out for final model evaluation.

This division was performed using train_test_split from the sklearn.model_selection module. The random seed was fixed (random_state=42) to ensure reproducibility across training runs and maintain consistent data splits. Dataset splitting was also done to prevent the multi-task model from overfitting.
3.3.5	Pre-processing and Augmentation Pipeline
Before the data was loaded into the model, extensive pre-processing was applied to standardize image dimensions, increase diversity, and reduce overfitting:

Image Resizing: All MRI images and corresponding masks were resized to a fixed dimension of 256×256 pixels using the transforms.Resize() function. This uniform size allowed for consistency during training and it matched the training requirements of the SwinUnet model.
Normalization: Image tensors were normalized to the range [-1, 1]. Normalization speeds up convergence by standardizing the input distribution, which benefits gradient-based optimization.
Data Augmentation: To increase dataset diversity and robustness, the following augmentations were applied:
Random Horizontal and Vertical Flips: Simulate different orientations.
Random Rotations (±30°): Introduce variability in angle and position.
Colour Jittering: Adjust brightness, contrast, saturation, and hue, although this had minimal effect given the grayscale nature of MRI scans.
These augmentations were implemented using PyTorch’s torchvision.transforms.Compose() pipeline and were applied consistently to both images and masks during training.

Conversion to Tensors: Both images and masks were converted into PyTorch tensors using transforms.ToTensor(). This step is crucial for model compatibility and Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) acceleration.
Mask Clipping: Post-transform, the mask pixel values were clamped to [0, 1]. This ensures binary representation, as expected by the segmentation loss function.
3.4 	Multi-task Model Architecture

The system is built upon a multi-task deep learning architecture, designed to simultaneously perform tumour classification and tumour segmentation on 2D brain MRI slices. Unlike traditional single-task networks, this architecture utilizes a shared backbone and two task-specific branches, enabling shared representation learning. This not only reduces training time and computational cost but also leads to improved generalization due to the mutual reinforcement of related tasks.

The model takes a single input, a pre-processed MRI slice and produces two outputs including a segmentation mask, identifying the exact tumour region in the image  and a class label, categorizing the tumour as either glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumour, or no tumour. The core of the architecture consists of two primary components, EfficientNet-B0 which was used as the classification branch and U-Net which was used as the segmentation branch. These two branches are trained at the same time using a shared input and the adaptive loss balancing algorithm. Figure 3.2 is a diagram showing the architecture behind the multi-task model used.
Figure 3.2:Multi-task Model Architecture
3.4.1	EfficientNet (Classification Branch)

EfficientNet-B0 served as the base classification model because of its optimality in terms of performance and lightness. As opposed to conventional CNNs, EfficientNet applies a compound scaling method that concurrently scales up the network's depth, width, and input resolution. Using this new scaling method, it can achieve greater accuracy using fewer parameters and less computation expense, which makes it highly suitable to deployment in GPU memory-limited environments.

In this project, the pre-trained EfficientNet-B0 model available in PyTorch’s torchvision model zoo was used. To modify it to the specific task, the final classification head of the model was modified to output four logits, corresponding to the four different tumour types targeted in the classification task.

To enhance learning and decrease training time, transfer learning was utilized. The early layers of the model that have learned universal image features were frozen, and the later layers were fine-tuned with labelled MRI images. This allowed the model to learn the domain-specific features of brain tumours without wasting the helpful general features learned from large-scale image datasets.

EfficientNet-B0 was incorporated into the whole pipeline of the multi-task learning project. It received the same pre-processed image inputs as the U-Net model being employed for segmentation. In this architecture, EfficientNet was tasked with making high-level predictions of tumour classification and augmenting the semantic segmentation provided by the segmentation branch.
3.4.2	SwinUnet (Segmentation Branch)

The segmentation task for this project was tackled with a transformer model from the MONAI library, which is a library dedicated to medical imaging. SwinUnet is particularly suited for medical image segmentation because it is an encoder-decoder model and also has skip connections that enable it to retain spatial features that are important for accurate segmentation. These architectural merits place it in a good position for tumour segmentation from MRI images.

In this implementation, the segmentation arm of SwinUnet received the same pre-processed input images used by the classification arm. The encoder part of the network is composed of a sequence of convolutional blocks with ReLU activations, interposed by downsampling methods like strided convolutions and max pooling in order to progressively decrease spatial dimensions and capture high-level features. Meanwhile, the decoder pathway recovers spatial resolution through transposed convolutions and upsampling blocks.

A defining feature of SwinUnet is the use of skip connections that directly link corresponding encoder and decoder layers. These connections allow spatial information lost during down sampling to be reintroduced during upsampling, improving the precision of the final segmentation output. The model’s output consists of a single-channel mask, which is passed through a sigmoid activation function. Pixel values greater than 0.5 are interpreted as tumour regions, while values below this threshold are considered background.

The  model was initialized with randomly assigned weights and trained  using a combination of dice loss and focal loss. These losses are particularly effective for medical segmentation tasks, as it addresses the issue of class imbalance by focusing on the overlap between predicted and ground-truth tumour regions, rather than relying solely on pixelwise accuracy.
3.5	Adaptive Loss Balancing Function

This project implemented an adaptive loss balancing algorithm during model training to ensure that both the segmentation and classification task were receiving equal attention during training and were both performing optimally. The algorithm works by dynamically adjusting task-specific losses based on uncertainty weighting. The following sections describe the objective, structure, implementation, and effectiveness of this adaptive loss strategy as applied in this project.
3.5.1	Objective of the Adaptive Loss

In the multitask model environment, the segmentation and classification task each have their own loss functions. The losses from these two tasks  converge at different rates so the objective of the loss balancing was to learn optimal weighting factors for each task’s loss, allowing both tasks to contribute meaningfully during training. This approach eliminates the need for manual tuning of loss weights and promotes a more stable and effective joint optimization of the network
3.5.2	Structure of the Combined Loss Function

The total loss used in this project combines two components: the dice loss and focal loss for the segmentation task and categorical cross-entropy loss for the classification task. These are weighted using two trainable parameters, logσ1 and logσ2, which represent the log uncertainties of the segmentation and classification tasks, respectively. A regularization constant λ was introduced and set to 0.01 to ensure numerical stability and meaningful contributions from both tasks. This formulation allows the model to focus more on the task with higher uncertainty at any point during training.
3.5.3	Implementation Details

The adaptive loss function was implemented in a separate AdaptiveLoss class with PyTorch. Both log uncertainty parameters were created as trainable variables within the model class. These were fed to the loss function and backpropagated through backpropagation along with model weights. The log_sigma1 and log_sigma2 values were clamped to a specific range to ensure stability during training. This provided numerical stability and kept the adaptive weights from growing very large or very small, which would produce unstable training dynamics.
3.5.4	Regularization Strategy

To further promote balanced learning, a regularization term was incorporated into the total loss. This term, defined as λ (logσ12 + logσ22), penalizes excessive scaling of the uncertainty parameters. This discourages the model from favouring one task over the other and encourages equal and consistent contributions from both classification and segmentation throughout the training process.
3.5.5	Outcome and Effectiveness

The adaptive loss balancing algorithm was utilized effectively to balance the training of the two tasks. At initial phases of training, segmentation loss dominated and thereby enabled the model to learn spatial boundaries that are needed for precise tumour delineation. At later stages of training, classification loss started dominating increasingly and thereby resulted in balanced optimization within the two branches. This adaptive approach resulted in better convergence behaviour, more stable learning curves, and superior final performance metrics for both the classification and segmentation tasks.
3.6	Model Training and Evaluation

The multi-task model was trained in an end-to-end manner to ensure optimization. This approached ensured that the model could learn to categorize tumour types(classification) and accurately segment tumour regions (segmentation) in a unified framework. The adaptive loss balancing algorithm was also incorporated during model training.
3.6.1	Training Configuration
To facilitate effective learning, a set of carefully selected training hyperparameters and techniques were applied:
Optimizer: The multi-task model made use of the Adam optimizer, which was chosen because of its adaptive learning rate.
Learning Rate: The learning rate was initially 0.001. It was chosen to provide a compromise between training convergence and stability.
Weight Decay: Weight decay of 1×10-4 was applied to prevent overfitting. This is L2 regularization that discourages very large weights and aids generalization.

Learning Rate Scheduler: A step-based learning rate scheduler (StepLR) was applied, which reduces the learning rate by a factor of 0.1 every five epochs. Gradual decay aids smaller weight updates as training proceeds, which helps achieve convergence.
Epochs: The model was trained over 70 complete iterations of the training dataset. This number was determined based on the available computation time and the need for timely convergence.
Batch Size: A batch size of 8 was used, balancing the available GPU memory constraints with the need for stable gradient estimates during optimization.

All training was conducted using the Pytorch framework and leveraged GPU acceleration via CUDA when available. This setup enabled efficient handling of large image data and accelerated model computations.
3.6.2	Training Process

During each epoch of training, the model underwent a structured procedure to ensure consistent optimization. The model was first set to training mode, enabling features such as dropout and batch normalization to function appropriately. For each batch, pre-processed MRI slices, their corresponding ground truth segmentation masks, and tumour type labels were retrieved from the training DataLoader. These inputs were passed through the multi-task model, which simultaneously produced the predicted segmentation output, classification logits, and the two learnable parameters that controlled the uncertainty-based loss weighting.

The adaptive loss function was then used to compute a single total loss value by balancing the segmentation and classification losses. This dynamic weighting ensured that both tasks contributed effectively during training. After calculating the loss, backpropagation was applied to compute gradients, and the optimizer adjusted the model's weights accordingly. Following the update, the learning rate was adjusted using the StepLR scheduler to refine the optimization process over time.
3.6.3	Validation and Monitoring

At the end of each epoch, the model was evaluated using a separate validation set to monitor its generalization performance. During this phase, gradient computation was disabled to reduce memory consumption and speed up inference. The adaptive loss function was again applied to compute validation loss, allowing a direct comparison with training loss. This monitoring helped identify signs of overfitting and provided a basis for implementing early stopping strategies if necessary. In order to host the trained multi-task model for real-time prediction, a backend system was built upon Flask, which is a Python web framework that is nicely lightweight and ideal for machine learning model hosting. The backend was built to expose an API called /predict that takes MRI scans, runs inference with the trained model, and returns predicted tumour class and segmentation mask. There were five major functional modules in the Flask backend:
Flask Server: The central web application that waits for incoming requests and routes them to the proper handlers.
Model Loader: Upon start up, the backend loaded the trained multi-task model from disk and placed it onto the correct computation device (CPU or GPU) for inference.

Pre-processor: This module made sure that any image coming in from the MRI was processed by the same pre-processing chain of resizing, normalization, and conversion to tensor that was used while training the model.
Inference Engine: The image was then passed into the model to produce two outputs: segmentation mask defining areas of tumour and classification logits for predicting tumour type.

Post-processor: This component applied final transformations to the raw model outputs. The segmentation mask was thresholded to produce a binary image, and the classification logits were converted into probabilities using the softmax function. These processed results were prepared for easy interpretation and frontend integration.
The backend provided a single prediction endpoint, accessible via a POST request to /predict. This endpoint was responsible for handling incoming MRI image files. When a request was received:
The image was extracted from the request payload and converted to a tensor.
The model was called to perform a forward pass using the pre-processed       image.
The classification output was processed to yield the predicted class label with corresponding confidence scores.
The segmentation output was converted into a binary mask that visually delineated the tumour area.
Both results were packaged into a structured JSON response, enabling seamless communication with the frontend.

This backend architecture allowed the system to support real-time tumour detection and classification within a reasonable processing time, serving as the interface between the multi-task model and the web application.

4.4	Development Methodology

The development methodology used for this project is the Iterative Waterfall model. This approach combines the  traditional Waterfall model with the flexibility of Agile practices. Like the Waterfall model, stages such as requirements gathering, data preparation, model design, training, and evaluation are carried out sequentially. However, the iterative component allows for returning to earlier stages when necessary, especially useful in machine learning projects that require frequent refinement and experimentation.

At the start, the project followed a linear path: identifying objectives, sourcing data, and defining a multi-task architecture capable of both tumour segmentation and tumour type classification. However, during model development, it became clear that earlier decisions, such as how the data was pre-processed or how the loss functions were weighted ,needed to be revisited. Model training required extensive experimentation, including fine-tuning the shared encoder, adjusting hyper-parameters, and rebalancing the segmentation and classification branches. The Iterative Waterfall model was ideal in accommodating these repeated improvements without disrupting the overall structure of the project.
The key phases of this methodology as applied to the project are outlined below:

Project Initiation: The project began with the identification of a medical imaging problem that required a multi-task solution, tumour segmentation and classification from MRI scans. The goals and expected outcomes were clearly defined, and relevant research literature and datasets were reviewed.

Project Planning: The planning phase involved selecting the model architecture (a shared encoder with separate segmentation and classification heads), tools (such as PyTorch, NumPy, and OpenCV), and resources (including GPU access). The structure of input data and expected outputs for both tasks were also clearly mapped out.

Project Execution: MRI data and corresponding tumour masks and labels were pre-processed, resized, normalized, and organized into suitable training and validation sets. The model architecture was implemented, integrating a dual-output design for handling both segmentation maps and class predictions simultaneously.

Iterative Development: After initial training, several iterations were made to improve performance. This included adjusting learning rates, trying different loss combinations (e.g., Dice loss + CrossEntropy), refining augmentation strategies, and revisiting how data was split.

Continuous Testing: Throughout the development, the model was evaluated using relevant metrics: Dice coefficient and IoU for segmentation, and accuracy,f1 score for classification. Performance results from each iteration informed the next round of adjustments.

Repeat and Iterate: During the course of the project life cycle, results from the evaluation metrics were used to refine the model. This loop continued until both tasks achieved satisfactory performance levels.

CHAPTER FIVE
SUMMARY, RECOMMENDATIONS AND CONCLUSION
5.1	Summary

Multi-task learning is an emerging field in machine learning with many interesting prospects. In this project multi-task learning was used to provide a unified architecture for brain tumour segmentation and classification.

However the problem typically associated with multi-task environments, is loss balancing among the tasks involved, in a way that ensures that no task is dominating the other during training. The adaptive loss balancing algorithm used in this project, presents a dynamic way of balancing task and ensuring optimality.

This project used EfficientNet-B0 for tumour classification and U-Net from the MONAI library for segmentation. The shared input and joint training approach allowed for mutual learning between tasks, while an adaptive loss balancing strategy based on task uncertainty was employed to dynamically assign appropriate loss weights to each task during training. Two publicly available standard datasets were used to support the model: the BraTS 2020 dataset (used for segmentation) and the Figshare brain MRI dataset (used for classification). Both datasets were pre-processed and combined into a unified format to facilitate joint training.

Due to hardware limitations, the model was trained over 70 epochs instead of the intended 100, which constrained its full potential. Nevertheless, the model was successfully trained and evaluated using IoU Score and Accuracy for segmentation and F1 score and accuracy for classification . These metrics showed a strong performance across both tasks indicating that the adaptive loss balancing algorithm was effective in balancing learning and optimization.

The final model was integrated into a real-time web application using Flask and React.js, enabling users to upload MRI scans and receive both classification and segmentation results in real time. This application represents a practical deployment of the system for real-world use, particularly in clinical settings with limited resources.
5.2	Recommendations
The following recommendations are made for future development and research:

Upgrade of Hardware Resources: During the process of training the model, it was discovered that the computational power required to train the model, in terms of RAM and storage was not available. This limited the number of epochs that was able to train from 100 to 70.

Expand Diagnostic Scope: The scope of this project is limited to only the segmentation and classification of tumours, future improvements to the project could include other diagnostic tasks such as tumour localization, or progression, thus enhancing the  usefulness to low resource clinical settings.

Accept other Imaging Modalities: Future iterations of the model should be able to support additional brain imaging modalities such as CT scans alongside MRI. This extension would improve the model’s applicability across a broader range of clinical scenarios, especially in settings where MRI may not be readily available. This idea was suggested during the evaluation phase  by Dr. Alex, the Director of Covenant University Medical Centre, who emphasized the potential impact of a multi-modal model in improving diagnostic flexibility and accessibility in real-world medical environments.
5.3	Limitations of the Study
The major limitations of this study include:
Limited computational resources, including slow GPU and small RAM reduced the number of epochs that the model could train leading to a reduced accuracy that affected the segmentation IoU score.

The multi-task model only accepts one type of scan input which is MRI, it is not multi-modal so it cannot provide diagnosis, for other types of brain scans such as CT scans, which are also commonly used.
5.4	Conclusion

This final year project was able to successfully segment and classify brain tumours in a real time web application environment. A unified MRI architecture was built by leveraging the architectural strengths of EfficientNet and U-Net, and addressing task imbalance through a dynamic adaptive loss balancing algorithm

Despite limitations in computational resources, the system achieved high accuracy and was integrated into a web application for real-time medical inference. The contribution of this work is significant in both academia and practical implications, especially in resource-constrained clinical settings.

With further optimization, enhanced hardware, and multi-modality, this system has the potential to become a critical tool in medical imaging and diagnostics. It also makes a valuable contribution to the field of multi-task learning and intelligent medical systems.

tables: Digital Imaging and Communications in Media
To gather and pre-process a comprehensive dataset of MRI brain scans for training and evaluating the model.

A publicly available MRI brain scan dataset, called BraTS was downloaded from Kaggle. A brain tumour dataset containing 4 folders namely: no-tumour, glioma tumour, meningioma tumour and pituitary tumour was also downloaded from Figshare. The images were pre-processed by resizing  to a standard size of  256x256. The pixel values were normalized and converted to the required format for training the model. The dataset was augmented by flipping, rotating and adjusting the intensity in order to increase diversity and prevent overfitting. The dataset was split into training, validation and test sets of 70%, 15% and 15% respectively.
To develop a multi-task model for brain tumour segmentation and classification with an adaptive loss balancing algorithm.

A shared encoder-decoder architecture was implemented using SwinUNet for segmentation and EfficientNet for classification. Task specific loss functions such as Dice loss for segmentation and Categorical cross-entropy loss for classification, were defined. The adaptive loss balancing algorithm that uses uncertainty based dynamic weighting to adjust task priorities in the model was implemented. The model was trained using the already pre-processed dataset, with backpropagation and Adam optimizer for parameter updates. The model was validated using cross fold validation and data augmentation to prevent overfitting.
To evaluate the performance of the multi-task model by benchmarking it against existing approaches for tumour segmentation and classification.

Performance metrics including : dice score and IoU (Intersection over Union) for segmentation, accuracy and f1 score for classification were used for assessment. The model was benchmarked against existing multi-task models for brain tumour segmentation and classification with standard datasets.
To integrate the multi-task model into a web application for real-time segmentation and classification of MRI brain scans.
The trained multi-task model was integrated into a web application with a Flask backend for real-time inference. React and Tailwind were used to develop the frontend of the website.
To evaluate the usability of the web application.
Post-Study System Usability Questionnaire standard questionnaires were issued to respondents in a clinical setting to analyse website usability and get user feedback.

Multitask learning (MTL) is a machine learning paradigm where a model is trained to perform multiple tasks simultaneously, with the idea that sharing information between tasks can lead to improved performance on each individual task. This paper presents a novel MTL approach that employs combined training for human activities with different temporal scales of atomic and composite activities. Atomic activities are basic, indivisible actions that are readily identifiable and classifiable. Composite activities are complex actions that comprise a sequence or combination of atomic activities. It can also help in providing a solution to the data scarcity problem by simultaneously learning multiple related tasks so that knowledge from each task can be reused by the others.
